title: New Species of Giant Armadillo Has Convoluted History - Nautilus
gist: A newly described glyptodont species, Glyptotherium deuterophractum — a giant armored armadillo relative the size of a Volkswagen Beetle that lived alongside early human migrants to South America — carries a taxonomic history that swung from 19th-century mythologizing to the first scientific description by Danish naturalist Peter Wilhelm Lund in 1837.

insights.claim: A newly named glyptodont species, Glyptotherium deuterophractum, is a giant armored armadillo relative from the megafauna that greeted the first humans to migrate into South America, with some glyptodonts reaching the size of a Volkswagen Beetle.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Adds a new named species to the Pleistocene South American megafauna record, relevant to paleontology and museum/collections research.

insights.claim: The taxonomic history of glyptodonts has been convoluted since their 19th-century discovery: writer Garcilaso de la Vega Inga speculated the fossils were remains of a giant human punished by God, some specimens were collected by Charles Darwin, and Danish naturalist Peter Wilhelm Lund gave the first scientific description of a glyptodont species in 1837.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Illustrates how pre-scientific mythological interpretation preceded rigorous taxonomy for major megafauna fossil finds, a recurring pattern in the history of paleontology.
insights.locator: When remains of these prehistoric beasts
